vjimc-2015-cat1-01.title: Substitute $x=\tan t$
vjimc-2015-cat1-01.body:
Let $\psi(t)=f(\tan t)$ for $t\in[0,\frac\pi4]$. As a composition of differentiable functions, $\psi$ is differentiable on $[0,\frac\pi4]$ with
$$\psi'(t)=f'(\tan t)\cdot\frac{1}{\cos^2 t}=\big(1+\tan^2t\big)\,f'(\tan t).$$
By Lagrange's mean value theorem there is $\xi\in(0,\frac\pi4)$ with
$$f(1)-f(0)=\psi\!\left(\tfrac\pi4\right)-\psi(0)=\frac{\pi}{4}\,\psi'(\xi)=\frac\pi4\big(1+\tan^2\xi\big)f'(\tan\xi).$$
Put $x=\tan\xi\in(0,1)\subset[0,1]$ and multiply by $\frac4\pi$:
$$\frac4\pi\big(f(1)-f(0)\big)=(1+x^2)f'(x).\ ∎$$

vjimc-2015-cat1-01.title: Cauchy's mean value theorem
vjimc-2015-cat1-01.body:
Let $g(x)=\arctan x$, so $g'(x)=\frac1{1+x^2}\neq0$ and $g(1)-g(0)=\frac\pi4$. By Cauchy's mean value theorem applied to $f$ and $g$ on $[0,1]$ there is $x\in(0,1)$ with
$$\big(f(1)-f(0)\big)\,g'(x)=\big(g(1)-g(0)\big)\,f'(x),\quad\text{i.e.}\quad \frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1+x^2}=\frac\pi4 f'(x).$$
Multiplying by $\frac{4(1+x^2)}{\pi}$ gives the claim. ∎

vjimc-2015-cat1-02.title: Powers of $\frac12$ off the diagonal
vjimc-2015-cat1-02.body:
**Yes.** Let
$$A=\left\{1,\tfrac12,\tfrac14,\tfrac18,\dots\right\}=\{2^{-k}:k\ge0\},\qquad B=\mathbb Q^+\setminus A .$$
Both sets are countably infinite ($\mathbb Q^+$ is countable, $A$ is infinite, and $B$ contains $3,5,7,\dots$). The diagonal cells $(i,i)$ form a countably infinite set, and so do the off-diagonal cells $(i,j)$, $i\ne j$.

Fix a bijection between $B$ and the diagonal cells and a bijection between $A$ and the off-diagonal cells, and fill the board accordingly. Then every positive rational appears exactly once.

Consider row $i$. It contains one diagonal number $b\in B$ and otherwise distinct numbers from $A$. Since all terms are positive, its sum is at most
$$b+\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}=b+2<\infty .$$
The same bound holds for every column. So the answer is **yes**. ∎

vjimc-2015-cat1-02.title: Any summable set works
vjimc-2015-cat1-02.body: The same idea works with any infinite set $A\subset\mathbb Q^+$ such that $\sum_{a\in A}a<\infty$, for example $A=\{1/n^2:n\ge1\}$. Put the elements of $\mathbb Q^+\setminus A$ on the diagonal, one per row and column. Put the elements of $A$ in the remaining cells, each exactly once. Each row or column then sums to one diagonal entry plus a subseries of a convergent series of positive terms. That sum is finite. ∎

vjimc-2015-cat1-03.title: Explicit multiple for $P$, root size for $Q$
vjimc-2015-cat1-03.body:
**$P$ divides such a polynomial.** Let $N=2015$ and $F(x)=1+x+\dots+x^{N-1}$. Then
$$P(x)F(x)=F(x)-2x^{N-1}F(x)+x^NF(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}x^i-2\sum_{i=N-1}^{2N-2}x^i+\sum_{i=N}^{2N-1}x^i .$$
Collect the coefficient of $x^i$:
- $0\le i\le N-2$: $1$;
- $i=N-1$: $1-2=-1$;
- $N\le i\le 2N-2$: $-2+1=-1$;
- $i=2N-1$: $1$.

So $P(x)F(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{N-2}x^i-\sum_{i=N-1}^{2N-2}x^i+x^{2N-1}$. All its coefficients are $\pm1$.

**$Q$ divides no such polynomial.** We have $Q(2)=2^{2015}-2^{2015}-1=-1<0$ and $Q(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. So $Q$ has a real root $\alpha>2$. Suppose $Q$ divides $G(x)=\sum_{j=0}^d g_jx^j$ with all $g_j\in\{\pm1\}$. Then $G(\alpha)=0$, so $g_d\alpha^d=-\sum_{j<d}g_j\alpha^j$. Taking absolute values,
$$\alpha^d\le\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\alpha^j=\frac{\alpha^d-1}{\alpha-1}<\alpha^d-1,$$
because $\alpha-1>1$. This is a contradiction.

**Answer: $P$ yes, $Q$ no.** ∎

vjimc-2015-cat1-03.title: Why the root bound is natural
vjimc-2015-cat1-03.body:
A polynomial $G=\sum_{j\le d}g_jx^j$ with $|g_j|=1$ cannot vanish at any $z$ with $|z|\ge2$. If $G(z)=0$, then
$$|z|^d\le\sum_{j<d}|z|^j=\frac{|z|^d-1}{|z|-1}\le |z|^d-1 .$$
So every root of such a $G$ lies in the disc $|z|<2$. Any divisor of $G$ must also have all its roots there.

Now $Q(2)<0<Q(3)$, so $Q$ has a root in $(2,3)$ and cannot be a divisor.

For $P$, this necessary condition gives no obstruction (note $P(2)=1>0$), and it is not sufficient anyway. The explicit product $P\cdot(1+x+\dots+x^{2014})$ from the first solution shows that $P$ really is a divisor. **Answer: $P$ yes, $Q$ no.** ∎

vjimc-2015-cat1-04.title: Roots-of-unity filter and induction on $v_p(m)$
vjimc-2015-cat1-04.body:
Write $f(x)=\sum_{\ell=0}^n a_\ell x^\ell$. We prove the following statement by induction on $v_p(m)\ge1$:

> **(S)** If $p\mid m$, $f\ne0$, $\Phi_m\mid f$ and $\deg f<\frac p{p-1}\varphi(m)$, then $f$ has at least $p$ nonzero coefficients.

Let $\varrho=e^{2\pi i/p}$. We use the standard fact
$$\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}\varrho^{jt}=\begin{cases}p,& p\mid t\\ 0,&p\nmid t.\end{cases}\tag{1}$$

**Base case: $m=pk$ with $p\nmid k$.** Then $\varphi(m)=(p-1)\varphi(k)$, so $n<p\,\varphi(k)$. We show more: *for every residue $r$ modulo $p$, some $a_\ell$ with $\ell\equiv r\pmod p$ is nonzero.* This gives at least $p$ nonzero coefficients.

The polynomial $\Phi_k(x^p)$ has degree $p\varphi(k)$. Its roots are the $p\varphi(k)$ distinct numbers $w$ with $w^p$ a primitive $k$-th root of unity. Each such $w$ has order $k$ or $pk$, because $\operatorname{ord}(w^p)=k$ and $p\nmid k$. If $f$ vanished at all of them, $\Phi_k(x^p)$ would divide $f\neq0$ and then $\deg f\ge p\varphi(k)>n$, which is impossible. So there is a root $w$ of $\Phi_k(x^p)$ with $f(w)\ne0$. Every element of order $pk=m$ is a root of $\Phi_m$ and hence of $f$, so $w$ has order exactly $k$.

Let $\varepsilon=e^{2\pi i/m}$, so $\varrho=\varepsilon^k$. Write $w=\varepsilon^{s}$. Since $\operatorname{ord}(w)=k=m/\gcd(s,m)$, we get $\gcd(s,m)=p$, so $s=ps'$ with $\gcd(s',k)=1$.

For $1\le j\le p-1$ consider $w\varrho^j=\varepsilon^{s+jk}$:
- A prime $q\mid k$ divides $k$ but not $s$, so $q\nmid s+jk$.
- The prime $p$ divides $s$ but not $jk$, so $p\nmid s+jk$.

Hence $\gcd(s+jk,m)=1$, so $w\varrho^j$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity and $f(w\varrho^j)=0$.

Fix $r$ and put $S=\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}\varrho^{-jr}f(w\varrho^j)$. Only the term $j=0$ survives, so $S=f(w)\ne0$. On the other hand, expanding $f$ and using (1),
$$S=\sum_{\ell=0}^n a_\ell w^\ell\sum_{j=0}^{p-1}\varrho^{j(\ell-r)}=p\sum_{\ell\equiv r\ (\mathrm{mod}\ p)}a_\ell w^\ell .$$
Since $S\neq0$, some $a_\ell$ with $\ell\equiv r\pmod p$ is nonzero. This proves the base case.

**Inductive step: $p^2\mid m$.** Write $m=pm'$ with $p\mid m'$. Then $m$ and $m'$ have the same prime divisors, and $\varphi(m)=p\,\varphi(m')$.

Group the terms of $f$ by exponent modulo $p$: $f(x)=\sum_{r=0}^{p-1}x^rf_r(x^p)$, where the coefficient of $x^i$ in $f_r$ is $a_{pi+r}$.

Let $\eta$ be any primitive $m'$-th root of unity and $\zeta$ any number with $\zeta^p=\eta$. If $d=\operatorname{ord}\zeta$, then $d/\gcd(d,p)=m'$. Since $p\mid m'$, $d=m'$ is impossible, so $d=pm'=m$. Thus $\zeta$ is a primitive $m$-th root of unity. The same holds for all $p$ numbers $\zeta\varrho^j$, $j=0,\dots,p-1$, since they also satisfy $(\zeta\varrho^j)^p=\eta$. Therefore
$$0=f(\zeta\varrho^j)=\sum_{r=0}^{p-1}\varrho^{jr}\,\big(\zeta^rf_r(\eta)\big),\qquad j=0,\dots,p-1 .$$
This is a linear system with the invertible Vandermonde matrix $(\varrho^{jr})$, so $\zeta^rf_r(\eta)=0$, i.e. $f_r(\eta)=0$ for all $r$. Because $\Phi_{m'}$ has simple roots, $\Phi_{m'}\mid f_r$ for every $r$.

Moreover $\deg f_r\le n/p<\frac{\varphi(m)}{p-1}=\frac{p}{p-1}\varphi(m')$. Since $f\ne0$, some $f_r\ne0$. By the induction hypothesis applied to $m'$ (with $v_p(m')=v_p(m)-1\ge1$), $f_r$ has at least $p$ nonzero coefficients. These are distinct nonzero coefficients $a_{pi+r}$ of $f$.

This completes the induction. In particular the given polynomial (which is nonzero because $a_n\ne0$) has at least $p$ nonzero coefficients. ∎

*Remark.* The bound is sharp: $\Phi_{p^2}(x)=1+x^p+\dots+x^{(p-1)p}$ has exactly $p$ nonzero coefficients. This example also shows why the residue-class statement can fail when $p^2\mid m$, and why the induction is needed.
